definition: Texturing treats smooth continuous-filament yarn to give it crimp, loops or bulk, making it softer, fuller, more opaque or stretchier than flat filament yarn.
explanation: Flat synthetic filaments pack tightly and feel slick, and texturing disrupts that parallel arrangement. In false-twist texturing the yarn is twisted, heated so that the twisted form is set, cooled and then untwisted; because the twist exists only between two points, the filaments emerge with a set, helical crimp that gives stretch and bulk. In air-jet texturing, overfed filaments pass through a turbulent air jet that forms stable loops and entanglements, producing a spun-like yarn with little stretch. Stuffer-box and knit-deknit methods are other routes.
example: A designer handles knit swatches made from the same polyester. The one from flat yarn is shiny, slippery and somewhat see-through; the one from false-twist textured yarn is matte, bulkier and stretches noticeably. A third, made from air-jet textured yarn, looks and feels closer to a spun-yarn fabric but lacks the stretch of the false-twist version.
caution: Textured does not mean staple: a textured yarn is still continuous filament and behaves differently from spun yarn in pilling and snagging. Texturing crimp is heat-set, so high temperatures in finishing, drying or ironing can relax it. The word also has an everyday meaning (a fabric's surface texture), so check whether a specification refers to the yarn process.
deeper: False-twist machines commonly draw and texture partially oriented yarn (POY) in one step, called draw texturing; one review states that this route handles about 60 percent of the world's melt-spun filament yarn. Reported settings include exit speeds of about 600 to 900 m/min, heater temperatures around 200 to 220 C for polyester, and a disc-to-yarn speed ratio of roughly 1.9 to 2.1 on friction-disc twisters. Heat and torsion partly disorient the polymer's supramolecular structure. A second heater can reduce stretch and torque to make 'set' yarns. Air-jet texturing depends on overfeed into the jet, and filament preheating is reported to improve loop frequency, stability and bulk.
origins: Texturing developed in the mid-twentieth century, once nylon and then polyester filament yarns were widely available, as a way to give them the stretch, comfort and cover associated with spun natural-fiber yarns. Early false-twist machines twisted yarn with rotating spindles; friction discs and belts later raised speeds, and research systems have replaced friction discs with water-jet twisters and steam heaters for texturing at up to about 1,500 m/min.

definition: Thread count is the number of warp ends plus weft picks in one square inch of woven fabric, most often quoted for bed sheets.
explanation: Weavers measure density separately in each direction: ends per inch or centimeter in the warp and picks per inch or centimeter in the weft. Thread count adds the two per square inch. Density interacts with yarn count: finer yarns allow more threads in the same space, while coarse yarns at high density would jam. Laboratories count threads with a pick glass or by raveling, on conditioned fabric away from the selvedge.
example: A percale sample shows 110 ends and 90 picks per inch, a thread count of 200. A competing label claims 400 for a fabric with a similar hand. Under magnification the second fabric shows about 100 ends and 100 picks, but each yarn is two-ply. The 400 figure comes from counting plies, not yarns. The two fabrics are closer in construction than their labels suggest.
caution: A higher thread count is not a quality guarantee. Counting each ply of a plied yarn as a separate thread can double or triple the number without adding any more yarns, which can mislead a buyer comparing labels. Ask for ends and picks per inch, yarn count and ply. Fiber quality, finishing, weave and fabric weight matter as much as density.
deeper: Warp and weft densities, together with yarn linear density, determine cover: the proportion of fabric area occupied by yarn. Two fabrics with the same density can differ in cover if one uses coarser yarn. Density also governs crimp, air permeability and tear behavior; tightly set fabrics resist abrasion but can tear more easily because yarns cannot bunch to share load. Published studies commonly report construction in these terms; for example, one comparison of plain, twill and satin fabrics used warp densities of 90 to 100 ends per inch and weft densities of 50 to 60 picks per inch. Standard test methods specify counting direction, specimen location and how many counts to average. Mass per unit area can be estimated from densities, yarn tex values and crimp.
origins: Recording ends per unit width is intrinsic to weaving, since the warp must be set through a reed with a fixed number of dents per inch. The single combined thread-count number became a retail marketing figure for household textiles, and disputes over how plied yarns should be counted followed. This edition could not verify the current text of any regulator's guidance, so readers should consult the relevant authority directly.

definition: A document issued by a certification body confirming that a specific shipment of goods, sold by a certified supplier, contains material certified to a named standard.
explanation: In Textile Exchange's certification system and similar schemes, a supplier holds a scope certificate showing that its site, processes and product categories are certified. That alone proves nothing about a particular sale. A transaction certificate fills the gap: the certification body issues it for a defined shipment, listing the products, quantities, shipment details, the buyer's name and address, and the certification status of the goods. Its details are expected to match invoices and shipping documents, and a TC is issued each time certified goods change ownership along the chain.
example: A brand receives a fabric delivery described as containing certified organic cotton. The fabric mill's scope certificate shows that it is certified, but the brand's reviewer also asks for the transaction certificate covering this delivery. Matching the TC's invoice numbers, net weights and product descriptions against the delivery paperwork is what connects the claim to the goods actually received.
caution: A TC confirms certified content and chain-of-custody status for one shipment under one standard, nothing more. It does not certify labor conditions, chemical use or environmental performance unless the standard itself covers them. Because TCs are generally issued after goods ship, buyers may have to wait; the testing and certification firm IDFL says the delay is often one to two weeks. Confirm authenticity with the issuing body.
deeper: Transaction certificates are the link records of a chain-of-custody system. During audits, each certified seller's inputs and outputs are reconciled, and the TC tells the next buyer what certified quantity it received, which in turn caps what that buyer may claim on its own outputs. Textile Exchange sets its rules in a Policy for Transaction Certificates (ASR-104), revised several times, including version 3.0 dated September 2021 and version 3.1 dated 1 October 2023. The policy governs when TCs are issued, what data they carry and how they relate to claim rules. Where a certified step lacks a TC, the documentary chain for downstream claims is generally broken, even if the material itself was never altered.
origins: The name describes its function: a certificate tied to one commercial transaction rather than to a company. Shipment-level certificates are also used in other certified supply chains, such as organic agricultural trade. Textile Exchange built TC requirements into the accreditation and certification procedures that support its content standards, including the Organic Content Standard and the Recycled Claim Standard, and the Global Organic Textile Standard uses transaction certificates in its own chain of custody.
